articles.title: My Claude Code workflows ran for days. Headless workers finished in minutes.
articles.excerpt: I run four projects with Claude Code. For a while, my long multi-agent jobs went through Claude Code's Workflow tool, and they kept running for days. Some never finished. Part of it was effort. Every…
articles.body: I run four projects with Claude Code. For a while, my long multi-agent jobs went through Claude Code's Workflow tool, and they kept running for days. Some never finished. Part of it was effort. Every agent in a workflow runs at the effort level of the session that started it, and a workflow script has no documented per-agent effort setting. So I kept switching model and effort by hand, trying to make the big jobs move. That became a job of its own. The setup that worked I split the roles. One interactive Claude Code session is the orchestrator. It plans the work, writes a narrow brief for each part, launches it, reads the report and decides what happens next. Each part runs as a headless claude -p worker in its own git worktree, with its own tool list, model, effort and budget.
articles.author: Ozgur Sagiroglu

articles.title: Designing Resilient Payment Microservices: Idempotency, Webhooks & Double-Entry Ledgers
articles.excerpt: A practical deep dive into handling mobile money STK pushes, preventing double-credits with distributed locks, and building robust ledger pipelines. Handling real-money transactions in backend microse…
articles.body: A practical deep dive into handling mobile money STK pushes, preventing double-credits with distributed locks, and building robust ledger pipelines. Handling real-money transactions in backend microservices comes with a harsh reality: networks fail, webhooks retry unpredictably, and duplicate requests will happen. Whether you are integrating mobile money APIs (like M-Pesa Daraja or IntaSend) or card processors, standard CRUD patterns fall short. If an STK Push takes 12 seconds to resolve on a customer's handset and the webhook delivers three identical callbacks within 500ms, your system must guarantee that customer balances, creator payouts, and platform accounts remain mathematically consistent.

articles.title: PostgreSQL Constraint Triggers for AI Feature Usage Quotas: Enforcing Hard Limits at the Database Layer
articles.excerpt: PostgreSQL Constraint Triggers for AI Feature Usage Quotas: Enforcing Hard Limits at the Database Layer I've watched quota systems fail at scale more times than I'd like to admit. You implement soft c…
articles.body: PostgreSQL Constraint Triggers for AI Feature Usage Quotas: Enforcing Hard Limits at the Database Layer I've watched quota systems fail at scale more times than I'd like to admit. You implement soft checks in FastAPI—verify the tenant hasn't exceeded their monthly Claude API calls, then call the API. Works fine locally. Ships to production. Then during a traffic spike, three concurrent requests all see the same usage_count = 45 from the database, all think they're under the 50-call limit, and suddenly you're processing 153 calls instead of 50. Application-layer quota enforcement is fundamentally racy. Every soft check you write is a time-of-check to time-of-use (TOCTOU) window waiting to bite you.
articles.author: Ugur Aslim

articles.title: Beyond Text Generation: The Rise of System One Models (Jev, OpenAI Decisions, and the 2026 Agent Control Plane)
articles.excerpt: Beyond Text Generation: The Rise of System One Models (Jev, OpenAI Decisions, and the 2026 Agent Control Plane) The artificial intelligence industry has arrived at a structural turning point in 2026:…
articles.body: Beyond Text Generation: The Rise of System One Models (Jev, OpenAI Decisions, and the 2026 Agent Control Plane) The artificial intelligence industry has arrived at a structural turning point in 2026: text generation is becoming the greatest bottleneck in software automation and autonomous agent execution . For the past three years, software engineering teams built AI agents by forcing Large Language Models (LLMs) to perform every cognitive operation through the narrow straw of autoregressive token streaming. Whether determining if a bash command is dangerous, selecting which database tool to invoke, rating customer sentiment, or checking if a pull request test failed, developers asked giant frontier models like GPT-4 or Claude to output sentences or stream JSON characters token-by-token.

articles.title: Doom 2016 Composer Mick Gordon Says "F##k AI"
articles.excerpt: Doom 2016 Composer Mick Gordon Says "F##k AI"
articles.body: Aussie composer Mick Gordon is highly regarded for his experimental approach to musical composition. For 2013's Killer Instinct he employed a kangling, a Tibetan instrument traditionally carved into a human femur or tibia, to build a theme for the skeletal Spinal character out of actual bones. For 2016's Doom he famously sampled real chainsaw noises to pull off the unique guitar riffs that elevated the game's soundtrack into a heavy metal masterpiece. However, when asked if he's considered incorporating any form of generative AI into his creative process, Gordon doesn't mince his words. To paraphrase the late Meatloaf, Gordon will do anything to create a great soundtrack, but he won't do that .
